newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO panel backs India in textile row with U.S.
newsitem.headline: WTO panel backs India in textile row with U.S.

text.p: A World Trade Organisation panel has found the United States violated free trade rules by slapping limits last year on imports of some woollen clothing from India, trade sources said on Monday.
The sources said the ruling was communicated to the two countries in mid-December and had been distributed to other WTO members -- now totalling 128 -- on Monday.

The import restrictions, which affected woven men's shirts and women's blouses, were introduced from April 1995 after the United States said a surge of these goods from India posed a threat of serious damage to domestic producers.
The restrictions were extended for a further 12 months in April last year but were withdrawn in December after U.S. officials said there had been a steady decline in imports.

India took the case, together with a linked complaint on U.S. limits imposed on woollen coats, to the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) after another WTO body, the Textile Monitoring Board (TMB), effectively sanctioned the U.S. move.
Indian officials argued before the three-member panel set up by the DSB last April that the unilateral restrictions ran against the 1994 world trade treaty and its Agreement on Textiles and Clothing.

The panel -- composed of experts from Belgium, Australia and Switzerland -- found that the U.S. measures had impaired India's rights under the pact, which also created the WTO to replace the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
There was no immediate indication in Geneva on whether the United States would appeal against the ruling, but diplomats said it was almost certain that it would.

Under the WTO's dispute settlement procedure, a DSB meeting to consider whether to approve the report can be called a minimum of 20 days from Monday and the United States will have to say 10 days before that whether it will appeal.

An appeals panel, which can look only at whether the argument of the original panel was based on correct legal reasoning and not at the substance of the case, would be expected to return its findings within 60 days.
If it also rules against Washington, the United States, would be asked to compensate India for its loss of trade while the limits were in force.
